newsitem.title: USA: Disney buys Pixar stock, sets five film deal.
newsitem.headline: Disney buys Pixar stock, sets five film deal.

text.p: Walt Disney Co. Monday agreed to purchase up to 5 percent of Pixar Animation Studios in a deal that gives the creator of the blockbuster film "Toy Story" a greater share of the profits from its films.
At a news conference, officials from both companies said they will become equal partners in five animated film projects over the next 10 years.
News of the deal sent shares of Richmond, Calif.-based Pixar up almost 49 percent, or $6.875, to close at $21 on Nasdaq.
Disney Chairman Michael Eisner said the agreement would allow the entertainment giant to remain the leader in animated films.
"I think this arrangement with Pixar demonstrates Disney's interest in being on the cutting edge of technology as it relates to creativity and story telling," Eisner said.
Under terms of the agreement Disney and Pixar will produce five movies over the next 10 years, starting with the animated feature "Bugs" which is slated for release in late 1998.

Eisner said the two companies will share equally in the costs of the projects and the profits, a far cry from Disney's earlier agreement under which Disney received the bulk of the proceeds from "Toy Story."

Officials from both companies said the change reflects a growing belief that Pixar is capable of repeating the success of "Toy Story" and concerns that another studio might try to lure Pixar away from Disney.

"We're not buying technology, we're not buying computers," said Peter Schneider, president of Walt Disney Feature Animation. "We're in a partnership with artists to make movies to which hopefully the technology is transparent to the viewers."

Pixar Chairman Steve Jobs, who also founded Apple Computer Inc., said Pixar was courted by a number of rival studios, but in the end it chose to remain with Disney because the arrangement has worked well so far.
"When we first got into the relationship (with Disney), a lot of people said 'be very careful, they're very difficult. But I haven't found that at all. In fact it's been just the opposite."
"I think there is a certain feeling that these are the guys we want to work with because they're the best, and why would we want to work with anyone else?" he added.
The two studios will be equal partners on the five pictures and related products, including home videos, merchandise, interactive- media products and made-for-home-video sequels.

Disney will purchase 1 million shares of Pixar's common stock at $15 a share. In addition, Disney will receive warrants to purchase an additional 1.5 million shares of Pixar common stock at higher prices. If the warrants are exercised, Disney will have a combined total of about 5 percent of Pixar.

Eisner said Disney had no plans right now to push for a reprsentative on Pixar's board of directors or to acquire a controlling stake in the company but he did not rule out additional stock purchases in the future.
Released in 1995, the film "Toy Story" was the first full-length feature animation produced entirely by computer.
To date, the film has grossed more than $350 million worldwide, and is projected to sell more than 30 million video cassettes around the world.
Disney stock closed up 25 cents at $75.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
